newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Supreme Court to review assisted-suicide laws.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Supreme Court to review assisted-suicide laws.

text.p: The Supreme Court will enter the nationwide controversy over doctor-assisted suicide on Wednesday in a case whose importance could rival the historic 1973 ruling that legalised abortion.
The U.S. high court will hear two hours of arguments on whether mentally competent, terminally ill patients have a constitutional right to seek help from their doctors in committing suicide.

The dispute, which raises profound legal, moral and ethical questions, has sparked a debate of the most emotional intensity of any issue since the landmark 1973 ruling in "Roe v. Wade" that women have a constitutional right to abortion.

"Remember how Roe v Wade changed America. It could happen again in January 1997," said the conservative Family Research Council, which filed a court brief opposing doctor-assisted suicide as "false compassion and a perversion of mercy."

At issue are laws from New York and Washington state that ban doctor-assisted suicide. More than 30 states have formally made assisted suicide a crime while only Oregon has allowed it. A Supreme Court ruling is expected by July.
A U.S. appeals court in California last year created a fundamental right to physician-assisted suicide, citing the same constitutional liberty protections used as the basis for the abortion ruling.

But University of Notre Dame law professor Douglas Kmiec predicted the Supreme Court likely would be inclined to "disentangle" abortion from assisted suicide "to avoid the jurisprudential controversies of the recent past."
The Clinton administration has rejected the view that the so-called right-to-die was similar to a woman's constitutional right to an abortion.

"The right to choose an abortion implicates a constellation of liberty and equality rights of fundamental importance that are not implicated here," Walter Dellinger, the administration's top courtroom lawyer, said.
In a brief filed with high court, Dellinger said: "Once a state decides to create an exception to its prohibition against assisted suicide, there is no obvious stopping point."
President Bill Clinton has repeatedly refused to support a right to doctor-assisted suicide.
Harvard University law professor Laurence Tribe, who will be arguing before the court in favour of assisted suicide, said it spares a terminally ill patient needless pain and agony.

"The person who is dying in intolerable pain or torment faces suffering that is too intimate and personal for the state to insist that (the patient) bear it," Tribe said in his brief. The decision must be left to the individual, he said.
Joining Tribe in arguing for assisted suicide will be Kathryn Tucker, an attorney for a Washington-based group called Compassion in Dying.

Dellinger will be joined by a lawyer for the state of Washington and New York Attorney General Dennis Vacco in defending the suicide bans. Vacco said a state has a legitimate interest in "protecting vulnerable patients from mistake and abuse."

The Supreme Court arguments do not involve Dr. Jack Kevorkian, a retired pathologist and America's best known advocate and practicioner of assisted suicide, who has publicly acknowledged attending over 40 deaths since 1990.
Two prosecutions against Kevorkian on state charges of assisted suicide are pending in Michigan.

The justices last addressed the right-to-die issue in 1990, ruling that a person has a constitutional right to refuse unwanted medical treatment in a case involving a comatose woman whose parents wanted to end artifical life support.
